summary.text: Bézout's identity says the greatest common divisor d of a and b can be written as a linear combination ax + by.
The two multipliers are called Bézout coefficients; they are not unique, and the extended Euclidean algorithm can compute a minimal pair.
It means any integer can be built from two coprime integers, and it decides exactly which water pouring puzzles are solvable.

facts.value: Étienne Bézout (1730-1783), who proved it for polynomials

items.prompt: What is 15(−9) + 69(2), and what does it show?

options.label: 1, because 15 and 69 are coprime
138, the larger of the two products
3, the greatest common divisor of 15 and 69
0, because the terms cancel out

items.explain: 15(−9) + 69(2) = 3, which is the greatest common divisor of 15 and 69 written as a linear combination of the two.

items.prompt: Can you reach every whole number by adding a whole-number multiple of 5 to a whole-number multiple of 9, with negatives allowed?

options.label: No, only numbers bigger than 45
No, only multiples of 5 or 9
Only the even numbers
Yes, since 5 and 9 are coprime

items.explain: Any integer can be written as a linear combination of two coprime integers: ax + by = 1, and multiplying both sides by n gives a(xn) + b(yn) = n.

items.prompt: Maya writes 3 as 15(−9) + 69(2), so (x, y) = (−9, 2). Her friend claims (x, y) = (14, −3) also gives 3. Can both be right?

options.label: Yes, the multipliers are not unique
No, only one pair can ever work
No, one of them must include a zero
Yes, but only for numbers under 20

items.explain: Bézout coefficients are not unique; (−9, 2) and (14, −3) are the two minimal pairs for this example.

items.prompt: 5 divides 20 evenly. Which simple choice of multipliers makes 5 times one number plus 20 times another equal their greatest common divisor?

options.label: 1 for the first and 2 for the second
1 for the first and 0 for the second
0 for the first and 1 for the second
4 for the first and -1 for the second

items.explain: When one number divides the other, the GCD is the smaller number, so 1 and 0 work: 5 times 1 plus 20 times 0 is 5.

items.prompt: The identity carries Bézout's name, though an earlier mathematician had the integer case. What further point does Andrew Granville make?

options.label: It was already implicit in Euclid's Elements: a misattribution
Bézout never proved anything at all about polynomials
The earlier statement was later shown to be wrong
The name was picked by Bézout himself back then

items.explain: Granville traced the naming to Bourbaki and argued that the identity is implicit in Euclid's Elements.
